newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan 97/98 draft budget focuses on cutting debt.
newsitem.headline: Japan 97/98 draft budget focuses on cutting debt.

text.p: Japan's cabinet on Friday approved a tighter state budget for the next fiscal year in an effort to put its debt-ridden fiscal finances in order.

With the economy finally set on a recovery path, the Ministry of Finance's (MOF) draft focuses on reducing the nation's accumulating debt instead of putting emphasis on strengthening the wobbly economic recovery.

Snowballing public debt and dwindling tax revenues have made Japan's budget deficit worse than those of major industrialised nations such as the United States, which is now actively engaged in trying to balance its budget.

The draft budget for the fiscal year starting next April stood at 77.39 trillion yen ($678 billion), up 3.0 percent from the original budget for the 1996/97 year, which in turn was 5.8 percent larger than the original budget for the 1995/96 year.
Japan will issue 16.71 trillion yen ($146 billion) worth of government bonds to help finance next year's budget.
The ministry allocated a record 21.03 trillion yen ($184 billion) worth of new government bonds in 1996/97, of which 12 trillion yen ($105 billion) were deficit-financing bonds.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka has said the government is aiming to cut bond issues, especially of deficit-financing bonds, by over four trillion yen ($35 billion), in order to achieve Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's goal of making 1997/98 the first year of fiscal reforms.
Hashimoto unveiled "Big Bang" financial reform plans last month to liberalise Japan's financial markets by 2001.

With the new issues, Japan will have depended on government bonds to finance 21.6 percent of its core budget at the end of March 1998, while the amount of outstanding government bonds at that time will total about 254 trillion yen ($2.22 trillion).

Japan has said that by the end next March it expects to have depended on bonds to finance 28 percent of this year's original budget, while outstanding government bonds will total 240 trillion yen ($2.10 trillion).
This will change to 28.8 percent and 241 trillion yen ($2.11 trillion) after an extra budget for the current fiscal year is enacted.
The cabinet on Friday also approved a draft supplementary budget totalling 2.67 trillion yen ($23.4 billion) for the year ending next March 31.
Tax revenues are estimated at 57.8 trillion yen ($507 billion) in 1997/98, up 12.6 percent from 51.35 trillion yen ($450 billion) in this fiscal year.

The ministry said the big revenue increase would be a result of a rise in the consumption tax to five percent from three percent in April, an end to special income tax cuts from January and expected economic growth of 1.9 percent in fiscal 1997/98.
These will boost tax revenues by about 6.4 trillion yen ($56.1 billion), a MOF official said.
On the expenditure side, the draft budget allocated 16.8 trillion yen ($147 billion) for debt servicing, up 2.6 percent from the original 1996/97 budget.
A government advisory panel said recently that Japan should aim for a "primary balance" of keeping spending -- excluding debt servicing costs -- below revenues in the next two to three years.
It also urged the government to keep the fiscal deficit at below three percent of gross domestic product by 2005.
"We were able to achieve primary balance in 1997/98," the official said.
General spending, the core of the budget, will total 43.81 trillion yen ($384 billion), up 1.5 percent from the amount earmarked in the original 1996/97 budget.
The senior MOF official said the planned consumption tax increase would boost government spending by about one percent, so the actual growth was minimal.
"Since the government forecast a 1.6 percent rise in the consumer price index (for 1997/98), nominal growth of 1.5 percent in general spending actually means no growth," he said.

Japan will raise defence spending by 2.1 percent to 4.95 trillion yen ($43.4 billion) in 1997/98. But the increase would be 1.98 percent if costs related to Special Action Committee on Okinawa, a team of U.S. and Japanese officials discussing the scaling back of U.S. bases there, are excluded.
Japan, the world's top aid donor, plans to increase funding for its official development assistance programme by 1.3 percent to 1.16 trillion yen ($10.1 billion).

Separately from the general account budget, the government's loans and investment programme -- funded by postal insurance, postal savings and other public funds -- will be 38.86 trillion yen ($340 billion) in 1997/98, down 4.1 percent from this year.
The draft budget is likely to be finalised on December 25, before being sent to parliament for approval in January.
